H1.text: A mango drops from a branch. A coin slips off a table. A drop leaves a tap.

H2.text: Three different things, one same pull from the Earth.

H3.text: Diya sees a mango fall from the tree outside her window. From four point nine metres, it lands in one second.

H4.text: Her puzzle: if the branch were twice as high, would the mango take two seconds?

H5.text: Most people say yes. By the end, you will see why the answer is no.

P2.text: So what is motion under gravity? When only gravity acts on a falling object, we call it free fall. We ignore the air.

P3.text: In free fall, every object speeds up at the same rate, called g, the acceleration due to gravity.

P4.text: Near the Earth's surface, g is about nine point eight metres per second, every second. It always points down.

P5.text: Heavy or light, without air they all gain speed at the same rate.

S1.text: Let's drop a mango from rest.

S2.text: After one second, it moves at nine point eight metres per second.

S3.text: After two seconds, nineteen point six. After three seconds, twenty nine point four.

S4.text: Every second, the speed grows by the same nine point eight. So the graph is a straight line.

S5.text: Slow-motion replay. Freeze at one second.

S6.text: The red arrow is g. It never changes. The blue arrow is the velocity. It keeps growing.

S7.text: Now the ghost copies. The gaps grow every second.

S8.text: First second, four point nine metres. Next second, fourteen point seven. Then twenty four point five. In the ratio one, three, five.

D1.text: Now the formulas, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. Take the equations of motion. The mango starts from rest, so u is zero, and a becomes g.

D3.text: Step two. v equals u plus a t becomes v equals g t. The speed grows in step with time.

D4.text: Step three. s equals u t plus half a t squared becomes h equals half g t squared. Height grows with time squared.

D5.text: Step four. v squared equals two g h. It gives the landing speed without the time.

T1.text: Remember this. In free fall, the acceleration is always g, pointing down. Speed changes. g does not.

K1.text: Side by side. A one kilogram stone and a five kilogram stone, dropped together with no air.

K2.text: The heavy one is pulled five times harder, but it is also five times harder to speed up.

K3.text: Now you try. Which stone lands first? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Together! The bigger pull and the bigger mass cancel, so both fall with the same g.

K5.text: Watch them fall. Both land at the same moment.

U1.text: Now throw a ball straight up at nineteen point six metres per second.

U2.text: Take up as positive. Gravity points down, so a is minus nine point eight.

U3.text: Each second it loses nine point eight metres per second. After two seconds, velocity is zero. That is the top.

U4.text: It has risen nineteen point six metres. Two seconds later it is back in your hand.

U5.text: Time up equals time down. It returns with the same speed, now pointing down.

U6.text: On the graph, one straight line slopes down, crossing zero at the top.

U7.text: Your turn. At the very top, the velocity is zero. Is the acceleration zero too? Pause and decide.

U8.text: No! It is still g, pointing down. If it were zero, the ball would just hang there.

W2.text: Back to Diya's mango. From four point nine metres, it takes one second. How long from nine point eight metres?

W3.text: Use h equals half g t squared. So t equals the square root of two h over g.

W4.text: Two times nine point eight, over nine point eight, is two. So t is the square root of two.

W5.text: That is about one point four one seconds, not two. Double the height, and the time grows only root two times.

X2.text: For a ball thrown up, many students take up as positive, yet write a equals plus nine point eight.

X3.text: Wrong. Pick one positive direction and keep it. If up is positive, a is minus g, both going up and coming down.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As numericals on stones dropped or thrown from towers.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A ball is thrown straight up at fifteen metres per second from a twenty metre tower. Take g as ten. When does it hit the ground? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is D. Four seconds.

A2.text: Up is positive. The ground is twenty metres below, so s is minus twenty.

A3.text: Minus twenty equals fifteen t minus five t squared. So t squared minus three t minus four is zero.

A4.text: So t is four, or minus one. Time cannot be negative. Three seconds is only the trip back to the top of the tower.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does a heavy stone not fall faster than a light one?

Y3.text: Two. What is the acceleration of a ball at the top of its flight?

Y4.text: Three. If the height becomes four times bigger, how much longer does the fall take?

N1.text: Next time: the mango's fall draws a curve on a graph. What does its shape tell you? We find out in position-time graphs.
